Brief Communications
Intrathecal baclofen for stiff-person
syndrome: Life-threatening intermittent
catheter leakage
J. Bardutzky, MD; V. Tronnier, MD; S. Schwab, MD; and H.-M. Meinck, MD
Abstract—Intrathecal baclofen (ITB) is used for unresponsiveness to other treatment for patients with stiff-person
syndrome (SPS). The authors report a patient with SPS who developed acute and life-threatening baclofen withdrawal
symptoms. Open surgery disclosed a small position-dependent leak in the catheter connector. This catheter failure was not
detected by standard noninvasive checking methods.
NEUROLOGY 2003;60:1976–1978
Stiff-person syndrome (SPS) is characterized by pro-
gressive rigidity of the axial and proximal limb mus-
cles and paroxysmal painful spasms precipitated by
various stimuli. Episodic life-threatening autonomic
dysfunction is often present,
1 and pathogenesis of SPS
is not fully defined, although an autoimmune-mediated
chronic encephalomyelitis may be the cause.
2 For pa-
tients who do not benefit from other treatment, intra-
thecal baclofen (ITB) is occasionally indicated.
3
Case report. After a 3-year history of progressive stiffness of
the axial and leg muscles and painful spasms, this 30-year-old
man was diagnosed with SPS in 1990. Antibodies against glu-
tamic acid decarboxylase (antiGAD-Ab) were present in serum
(167,000 RIA [U]) and CSF (2,459 RIA [U]). Oral clonazepam,
baclofen, tizanidine, and valproic acid were not helpful. Immuno-
modulation treatment with corticosteroids, plasmapheresis, and
IV immunoglobulins achieved only temporary improvement. As
the disease progressed, the patient’s overall mobility declined con-
tinuously, and at age 35 years, he was mostly confined to a wheel-
chair. In December 1996, a programmable pump device
(Synchromed, Model 8615, Medtronic Inc., Minneapolis, MN) for
continuous ITB infusion was implanted. ITB resulted in a long-
lasting improvement, and the patient was able to walk short dis-
tances without crutches. During the first 2 years, the daily dosage
had to be gradually increased from 220 /H9262gt o6 3 2/H9262g to suppress
the spasms sufficiently. A stable period with a maintenance dos-
age of 632 /H9262g/d for some years followed. In December 2000, the
pump had to be replaced because of battery depletion. His mobil-
ity had remained stable during the past 5 years, and no substan-
tial autonomic disturbance was reported.
One day before admission, the patient developed progressive
bilateral leg spasms with a jerky onset. Spasms were elicited by
various stimuli, spread gradually to the back, abdomen, neck, and
arms, and frequently occurred in series with short pauses. Spas-
modic attacks were accompanied and often preceded by profuse
diaphoresis, hyperthermia (41 °C), arterial hypertension (210/110
mm Hg), and tachycardia (160 beats/min). Initially such attacks
lasted for up to 5 minutes, but within hours turned into an almost
continuous spasmodic storm. Repeated IV boluses of 10 mg diaze-
pam did not interrupt the spasmodic storm or the autonomic dis-
turbance. Progressive involvement of the diaphragm led to
respiratory failure; thus, mechanical ventilation was inevitable.
Despite the immediate infusion of midazolam (45 mg/h) and the
muscle relaxant atracurium (60 mg/h), the jerky spasms could not
be adequately suppressed, resulting in rhabdomyolysis with an
increase in serum creatine kinase levels (29,482 U/L). Within 1

day, his clinical condition deteriorated dramatically, and multior-
gan dysfunction developed, including arterial hypotension, cardiac
infarction and heart failure, renal failure, pneumonia, metabolic
acidosis, and disseminated intravascular coagulation. Meningitis
and sepsis were excluded by normal CSF analysis and repeated
blood cultures. Because continuous, severe spasms developed as
soon as the myorelaxant was reduced, failure of the ITB delivery
system was suspected.
The pump was checked to exclude an error in programming or
in the filling status of the pump or the concentration of the ba-
clofen solution (2,000 /H9262g/mL). CSF could be aspirated easily
through the side port. Biplanar radiographic films showed that
the pump and catheter were in place. Programming a bolus to
produce a rotor movement of 90° demonstrated regular rotor func-
tion, and after an injection of 5 mL radiopaque solution through
the access port, the contrast medium entered the subarachnoid
space at the tip of the catheter without any obvious leakage.
On the supposition that the pump system was working cor-
rectly, the daily ITB dosage was gradually increased from 632 /H9262g
to 1200 /H9262g; however, this did not produce any significant improve-
ment. With high doses of sedatives and myorelaxants and the full
use of intensive care treatment, including dialysis and hemofiltra-
tion (3 weeks), mechanical ventilation (5 weeks), high-dose cat-
echolamines, and substitution of various blood components, the
patient’s clinical status stabilized, and he slowly began to recover.
Continuous IV administration of midazolam was replaced by an
oral medication of 3 /H110032 mg clonazepam, but the general muscle
stiffness could not be suppressed adequately, and the attacks of
myoclonic jerks and painful spasms required repeated IV boluses
of 0.5 mg clonazepam. Thus, surgical exploration of the pump
system was planned as soon as the patient’s condition had stabi-
lized sufficiently.
Open surgery revealed a small fissure in the catheter immedi-
ately beside the connector to the pump. Leakage of the drug oc-
curred only at a definite bending of the catheter (figure).
After surgical restoration of the catheter, ITB treatment was

continued with an initial dosage of 500 /H9262g/d. Motor and autonomic
disturbances rapidly improved to the state before admission, and
the patient was discharged after a 70-day hospital stay.
Discussion. Symptomatic treatment of SPS with
ITB has been reported to be effective in several stud-
ies3,4 and is now increasingly being used for patients
who do not respond to oral medication. However, inter-
ruption of ITB in spastic and particularly in SPS pa-
tients may cause severe and potentially fatal
withdrawal symptoms.
5-7 In our patient, symptoms of
baclofen withdrawal comprised severe hyperthermia
and violent attacks of jerky generalized muscle
spasms, including the diaphragm. Spasmodic episodes
were accompanied by sympathetic hyperactivity, even-
tually leading to autonomic failure and multiorgan dys-
function. Thus, ITB treatment of patients with SPS
must be considered potentially hazardous. Careful se-
lection of patients, close monitoring, and highly quali-
fied personnel are indispensable.
The pathophysiology of autonomic failure in SPS
patients is not fully understood. More than 60% of
SPS patients show signs of autonomic disturbance,
and 10% die suddenly, mostly because of autonomic
failure.
1,2 Acute withdrawal of ITB may induce auto-
nomic failure by uncovering or increasing the tendency
of SPS patients toward spontaneous disturbances in
the autonomic nervous system.
When acute hypertonicity develops in any patient
with ITB, acute withdrawal must be considered,
evaluated, and managed rapidly. If ITB withdrawal
is suspected, large oral doses of baclofen or, if not
feasible, IV benzodiazepines should be given immedi-
ately until restoration of ITB therapy.
A small fissure, which allowed leakage of the drug
only at a definite flexion of the catheter, caused the
withdrawal syndrome in our patient. Most likely, the
fissure was initiated during the pump replacement
while tightening a suture around the catheter. Possi-
bly, this particular condition reduced but did not
completely interrupt ITB delivery, thereby avoiding
a fatal course. The patient’s catheter was 5-years-old,
and barium-impregnated catheters may become brittle
after 5 to 10 years. Thus, surgeons should consider
replacing them at the time of pump replacement.
Malfunction of the catheter system may occur in
up to 40% of patients receiving ITB.
8 As shown in
this and other case reports, the reason may be diffi-
cult to identify
9,10 and requires a check of the whole
system according to an established protocol (table).
Our patient illustrates that noninvasive checking
methods may fail (see also reference 9). Small holes,
kinks, and fibrosis of the catheter can often only be
detected by surgery. In 20% of instances, however,
even surgery fails to identify the cause of system
malfunction, but replacing the catheter still restores
the clinical response to ITB.

CME Clinical aspects of MuSK antibody
positive seronegative MG
D.B. Sanders, MD; K. El-Salem, MD; J.M. Massey, MD; J. McConville, MRCP; and A. Vincent, FRCPath
Abstract—Serum antibodies to muscle-specific receptor tyrosine kinase were detected in 12 of 32 patients with general-
ized seronegative MG. All were women, with onset between ages 21 and 59 years. Seven had prominent neck, shoulder, or
respiratory muscle weakness and little or delayed ocular muscle involvement. The response to cholinesterase inhibitors
was variable, and electromyographic findings suggested myopathy in several. None improved after thymectomy. All
patients improved after plasma exchange, and most had a good response to selected immunotherapy. MuSK antibody
status should help diagnose MG with atypical presentations and ensure appropriate patient treatment.
NEUROLOGY 2003;60:1978 –1980
Up to 20% of patients with generalized MG do not
have detectable antibodies to the acetylcholine recep-
tor (AChR).
1,2 Evidence that “seronegative” MG
(SNMG) is an antibody-mediated disorder includes
passive transfer to mice, binding of immunoglobulin
(Ig) G to muscle cells, modulation of AChR function
or expression by seronegative plasma, transient neo-
natal myasthenia in babies born to seronegative
mothers, and improvement after plasma exchange
(see reference 2 for review). Although clinical charac-
teristics of SNMG are similar to those of seropositive
MG (SPMG), subsets of SNMG patients have pre-
dominant oculobulbar weakness and poor response
to therapy.
3,4
It was recently reported that sera from 71% of 24
SNMG patients contained antibodies to muscle-
specific tyrosine kinase (MuSK),
5 a surface mem-
brane receptor essential for the development of the
neuromuscular junction. Subsequent studies re-
ported that SNMG patients with antibodies to a 110
kDa protein, identified as MuSK, have more oculob-
ulbar weakness and a variable response to cholinest-

erase inhibitors, frequent respiratory crises, and no
benefit from thymectomy (A. Evoli et al., unpub-
lished observations).
6 Anti-MuSK antibodies have
not been found in ocular myasthenia (J. McConville
and A. Vincent, unpublished observations) nor in
SPMG.
7
This study was performed to determine the clini-
cal characteristics and response to therapy of our
patients with MuSK antibodies.
Methods. The Duke University Institutional Review Board ap-
proved this study. Sera were obtained from 32 consecutive pa-
tients with generalized SNMG seen in the Duke University
Medical Center MG Clinic during their first or follow-up visit.
Binding antibodies to the AChR had been measured before
thymectomy or immunosuppressive therapy and at least 6 months
after symptom onset. Twenty-eight patients were immunosup-
pressed. Sera were also obtained from 12 patients with general-
ized MG who had elevated binding antibodies to AChR (SPMG)
and from 7 seronegative patients with purely ocular weakness.
Sera were coded so that the testing laboratory was blinded to the

MuSK assay technique. MuSK antibodies were measured by

100 /H9262l, followed by immunoprecipitation with sheep anti-human

All positive sera were reassayed to confirm positivity, and serial
dilutions were tested to provide accurate titers.
Results. Anti-MuSK antibodies were found in 12 of 32 patients
with generalized SNMG but not in those with purely ocular myas-
thenia or SPMG. All MuSK-positive patients were women, with
MG symptom onset before age 60 years (table). Maximum disease
severity varied from mild (MGFA class IIA)
8 to crisis. Five had
typical MG findings, i.e., fluctuating ocular and oropharyngeal
symptoms. The others initially had proximal muscle weakness or
respiratory insufficiency without ocular symptoms. Most had
weakness limited to a few muscles, particularly neck extension,
shoulders, and respiration.
Electrophysiologic findings were unusual. In five MuSK-
positive patients, EMG demonstrated short duration, excessively
recruited motor unit action potentials in proximal muscles and
scattered fibrillations and repetitive discharges, consistent with a
necrotizing myopathy. Biopsy of deltoid muscle in four of these
patients showed only muscle fiber atrophy. EMG of weak muscles
was normal in the other patients.
Repetitive nerve stimulation was normal in a hand and shoul-
der muscle in four patients and produced a 10% decrement in both
muscles in one and a decrement greater than 10% only in the
shoulder in one. Jitter was normal in the extensor digitorum com-
munis (EDC) in six MuSK-positive patients and in the EDC and
frontalis in two who had weakness mainly in neck extension.
Jitter was markedly abnormal in neck extensor muscles in these
two patients. In a third patient, who had weakness mainly in
shoulder and neck muscles, jitter was normal in the EDC, moder-
ately increased in the frontalis, and markedly increased in the
deltoid.
Response to treatment. Responses to treatment were also not
typical of MG. Five MuSK-positive patients improved on pyri-
dostigmine; three did not; and one became worse. Thymectomy
was performed in seven patients. None had thymoma. All have
been followed for at least 8 months after surgery without definite
clinical benefit from thymectomy. Ten received plasma exchange
with dramatic improvement. Five improved with high-dose daily
prednisone. Four took therapeutic doses of azathioprine for at least 6
months, without improvement. Nine improved with cyclosporin or
mycophenolate mofetil. Five of these became asymptomatic.
Discussion. MuSK antibodies were found in 38%
of our patients with generalized SNMG; most were

immunosuppressed. All were women. Clinical pre-
sentation and EMG findings were typical for and
indistinguishable from SPMG in fewer than half of
the patients. The majority had weakness in a distri-
bution unusual for MG, sparing the ocular muscles
and predominantly involving neck, shoulder, and re-
spiratory muscles. In five patients, EMG findings
suggested myopathy, although this was not borne
out by muscle biopsy. In three patients, increased
jitter was found only or predominantly in neck ex-
tensor or shoulder muscles. This distribution is dif-
ferent from MG, in which abnormal jitter is almost
always found in arm or face muscles, or both.
MuSK antibodies have been reported previously in
71%
5 and 64%6 of patients with generalized SNMG.
Immunosuppression, which had been used in 28 of
our 32 patients, may have reduced the incidence of
MuSK positivity. However, MuSK antibodies tend to
be found in more severe disease, as was the case for
most of the patients in the first study,

to 40%,2 as found here. We found no correlation be-
tween the anti-MuSK antibody level and maximum
disease severity, but this may also have been af-
fected by immunosuppression.
Many previously described MuSK-positive pa-
tients had severe oculobulbar weakness and re-
sponded poorly to treatment.
6 We did not find this
clinical pattern in any of our MuSK-positive pa-
tients. Thus, it appears that MuSK antibodies may
be associated with at least three distinct clinical pre-
sentations: one that is indistinguishable from SPMG;
one with severe oculobulbar weakness; and one with
predominantly neck, shoulder, and respiratory mus-
cle weakness, with little or delayed ocular muscle
weakness. Two patients with anti-MuSK antibodies
have been reported to have profound muscle wasting
(J. Newsom-Davis, M.E. Farrugia, P. Anslow, R.
Kennett, A. Vincent, unpublished observations); al-
though five of our patients had myopathic features,
none had obvious muscle wasting.
As in previous reports, our MuSK-positive pa-
tients had a variable response to cholinesterase in-
hibitors; none who underwent thymectomy had
apparent benefit from the surgery, and improvement
after plasma exchange was consistently dramatic.
They differ in that most of our patients ultimately
had a good response to treatment, possibly because
of early, aggressive, and selected immunotherapy.
MuSK-positive patients with weakness only or
predominantly in neck and shoulder muscles could
easily be misdiagnosed. Assay for MuSK antibodies
promises to be of value in confirming the diagnosis
for these patients and for other patients with SNMG.
It may also be useful for selecting therapy.

Cervical cord dysfunction during neck
flexion in Hirayama’s disease
D. Restuccia, MD; M. Rubino, MD; M. Valeriani, MD, PhD; M. Mirabella, MD, PhD;
M. Sabatelli, MD; and P. Tonali, MD
Abstract—Neck flexion may play a role in the pathogenesis of Hirayama disease. Upper limb somatosensory evoked
potentials were recorded in five patients with Hirayama disease, six patients with ALS, and 14 healthy subjects. Neck

flexion caused a significant amplitude decrease of the N13 cervical response only in patients with Hirayama disease.
Direct cord compression or microvascular changes can in theory account for this position-related dysfunction.
NEUROLOGY 2003;60:1980 –1983
Hirayama disease is characterized by slowly progres-
sive distal amyotrophy of upper limb, usually mono-
lateral, occurring predominantly in young men.
1 In
the past, this disease was considered as a very mild
form of motor neuron disease. Recently, Hirayama et
al.
2 suggested that this disease could be due to tran-
sient cord compression occurring only during neck
flexion, but other investigators failed to find specific
features of flexion myelopathy.
3,4 Therefore, it would
be extremely relevant to demonstrate that neck flex-
ion causes functional modifications of the cervical
cord. The recording of the cervical N13 somatosen-
sory evoked potential (SEP) has proven useful in
revealing cervical cord dysfunctions.
5-7 Amplitude de-
crease of this potential usually reflects neuronal loss
in central gray matter; however, such an abnormal-
ity can also be caused by reversible inactivation of
dorsal horn cells, possibly due to microcirculatory

14 healthy volunteers and to six patients with ALS.
Methods. Subjects. All patients (table 1) showed weakness
and atrophy in the hand and forearm muscles, sparing the brachi-
oradialis. Neurologic examination did not reveal sensory distur-
bances, cranial nerve involvement, pyramidal signs, or urinary
disturbances. Electromyography showed denervation to the upper
limbs; nerve conductions were within normal limits. Patients with
ALS (3 men, 3 women; age range, 41 to 71 years, mean 60.8 years)
showed weakness and hypotrophy at upper and lower limbs, mild
bulbar signs, and enhanced tendon reflexes. Finally, SEPs were
recorded from 14 healthy subjects (6 men, 8 women; age range 20
to 44 years, mean 27.7 years).
Somatosensory evoked potential study. SEP recording proce-
dure has been described in detail in previous papers. Electrical
stimulations were delivered at the wrist for the median nerve
SEPs and above the ulnar groove at the elbow for ulnar nerve
SEPs. For patients with Hirayama disease, right and left upper
limb SEPs were obtained from three patients; in the remaining
two patients SEPs were recorded after stimulation of the more
symptomatic side. SEPs from control subjects and patients with
ALS were obtained after stimulation of median and ulnar nerves
on the right side. We measured the peaking latencies of Erb point
N9, cervical N13, root potential N9 recorded from the cervical
array, scalp far-field P14, and parietal N20. The amplitude of the
cervical N13 response was evaluated from the cervical traces us-
ing the N13/P9 amplitude ratio.

embolism after air travel
F. Lapostolle, MD; S.W. Borron, MD, MS; V. Surget, MD; D. Sordelet, MD; C. Lapandry, MD; and
F. Adnet, MD, PhD
Abstract—Prolonged air travel is associated with an increased incidence of thromboembolic events. The occurrence of
stroke was studied in patients with pulmonary embolism after air travel in a review of all flights arriving at Charles de
Gaulle Airport in Paris during an 8-year period. Thromboembolic stroke and patent foramen ovale were diagnosed in four
patients with pulmonary embolus.
NEUROLOGY 2003;60:1983–1985
Thromboembolic events, such as pulmonary embo-
lism and deep venous thrombosis, have been increas-
ingly recognized as complications of air travel,
particularly travel of long duration.
1,2 Other throm-
boembolic events related to prolonged air travel are
less well documented.
3,4 Neurologic deficit and im-
pairment of consciousness are unusual clinical pre-
sentations of patients with pulmonary embolism. We
undertook a descriptive study of patients with this
clinical presentation.
Methods. We previously studied passengers arriving at Charles

de Gaulle Airport in Paris with pulmonary embolism following air
travel during the period 1993 to 2000.1 In this study, patients with
suspected pulmonary embolism requiring care and transport to
hospital by French medical transport teams (SAMU) were system-
atically reviewed. Consecutive patients, admitted to 18 different
hospitals, were included upon confirmation of the diagnosis of
pulmonary embolism diagnosis by scintigraphic-ventilation perfu-
sion scanning, angiography, or high-resolution helical CT angiog-
raphy. Using the same methods, we extended the study period to
include 2001. During the 8-year study period, 155 million passen-
gers landed at Roissy Charles de Gaulle Airport. Among 65 pa-
tients with pulmonary embolus transported by SAMU after air
travel, four cases of cerebrovascular accidents were observed.
Stroke was diagnosed as focal neurologic deficit(s) associated with
acute ischemic infarct on CT scan. The medical records of these
four patients were specifically reviewed in order to describe their
clinical presentation.
Case 1. A 53-year-old woman with a medical history of two
pulmonary emboli, after abdominal surgery and during a postpar-
tum period, traveled by air from Los Angeles to Paris (9,080 km,
10.5 hours). She was under estrogen therapy for postmenopausal
symptoms. On arrival, in the jetway, she developed severe malaise
associated with pallor and diaphoresis. On clinical examination by
an emergency physician at the scene, she was noted to have im-
pairment of consciousness with complete left hemiplegia and left
facial paralysis. Blood pressure was 125/45 mm Hg, heart rate
was 105 per minute, and arterial oxygen saturation by pulse oxim-
etry was 69% on 10 L oxygen per minute. The patient was admit-
ted to an intensive care unit, where bilateral pulmonary embolism
was diagnosed by scintigraphic ventilation perfusion scan and
deep venous thrombosis was diagnosed by ultrasonography. Brain
CT scan revealed a massive right sylvian fissure thromboembolic
infarction with edema and mass effect. Transesophageal contrast

(120 pack-years) traveled from Rio de Janeiro to Paris (9,170 km,
11 hours). In the plane, standing up before landing, she developed
confusion and malaise. Clinical examination, performed by an
emergency physician on arrival in the airport, revealed an im-

Blood pressure was 120/70 mm Hg, heart rate was 100 per
minute, and oxygen saturation by pulse oximetry was 85% on
room air. She was admitted to an intensive care unit, where a
diagnosis of bilateral pulmonary embolism was confirmed by scin-

Transesophageal contrast echocardiography revealed a patent fo-

The patient was discharged home on day 30 with persistent apha-

Case 3. A 51-year-old woman, with no significant medical
history or cardiovascular risk factors, traveled by air from Phnom
Penh, Cambodia, to Paris (via Bangkok, 9,450 km, 11.25 hours).
In the plane, before landing, she developed dyspnea, malaise, and
a decreased level of consciousness. Clinical examination per-
formed by an emergency physician on arrival in the airport re-
vealed coma and left hemiplegia. Blood pressure was 120/80 mm
Hg, heart rate was 120 per minute, and pulse arterial oxygen
saturation was 88% on room air. She was admitted to an intensive
care unit, where a diagnosis of bilateral pulmonary embolism was
confirmed by high-resolution helical CT. Brain CT scan revealed a
massive left sylvian fissure thromboembolic infarct. Transesopha-
geal contrast echocardiography showed a patent foramen ovale.
This paradoxical embolism associated with severe pulmonary em-
bolism after air travel was treated with low-weight-molecular hep-

she died on hospital day 3.
Case 4. A 56-year-old man with no significant medical history
or reported cardiovascular risk factors traveled by air from New
York to Paris (5,840 km, 8 hours). In the plane, 3 hours before
landing, he developed malaise and impaired consciousness. Clini-
cal examination was performed by an emergency physician on
arrival in the airport. The examination revealed a coma with right
hemiplegia and aphasia. Blood pressure was 120/70 mm Hg, heart
rate was 70 per minute, and pulse oximetry showed a saturation
of 95% on 3 L oxygen per minute. He was admitted to an intensive
care unit. Brain CT scan and MRI revealed complete sylvian left
fissure thromboembolic infarct and mass effect. Transesophageal
contrast echocardiography showed patent foramen ovale. The pa-
tient was treated with low-weight-molecular heparin. Nine
months later, he remained in a rehabilitation unit with a persis-
tent hemiplegia and aphasia.
Discussion. Stroke due to paradoxical embolism is

apparently an unusual thromboembolic event after
prolonged air travel, having never, to our knowledge,
been reported in the literature. Among 65 patients
with pulmonary embolism after air travel, four cases
(6%) were associated with ischemic stroke. The
mechanism is presumed to be paradoxical embolism
as patent foramen ovale was demonstrated by echo-
cardiography in all four cases and other cause of
stroke was not found. However, the number of
strokes was small and echocardiography was per-
formed in only 45% of the patients with pulmonary
embolism
1; hence it was not justifiable to compare
four stroke patients against nonstroke patients to
determine whether the presence of patent foramen
ovale was statistically significant as a risk factor. It
is known that 30% of the normal population and an
estimated 39% of patients with pulmonary embolism
have a patent foramen ovale,
5-7 but the incidence of
ischemic stroke in the latter group has not been de-
termined to our knowledge. When air travel is in-
volved, our study suggests that about 6% of patients
with pulmonary embolism are at risk for stroke. We
can speculate that between 30 and 39% of the 65
patients had a patent foramen ovale or 19 to 26
patients among whom four had strokes. If the patent
foramen ovale was the key for the development of
stroke in the four patients, as seems reasonable, the
risk for stroke in the patients with pulmonary embo-
lism and patent foramen ovale would be somewhere
between four in 19 and four in 26, or approximately
15 to 21%. Although this figure is based on specula-
tion, it is a substantial percentage. We believe such
results suggest that patients who develop pulmonary
embolism after prolonged air travel and have patent
foramen ovale are at increased risk for paradoxical
embolism and ischemic stroke. Furthermore, this
may be an underestimate for two reasons. First of
all, patients who died for any reason, including se-
vere cerebral infarction and pulmonary embolism,
during or immediately after air travel were not in-
cluded in our study. Second, among patients whose
principal clinical presentation was characterized by
neurologic impairment, pulmonary embolism may
have gone undiagnosed.
In patients with patent foramen ovale, pulmonary
embolism suddenly increases right-sided heart pres-
sure, leading to a right-to-left atrial shunt that may
result in paradoxical embolism and stroke. Patent
foramen ovale has been demonstrated to be associ-
ated with a poor prognosis in patients with severe
pulmonary embolism.
8 Of note, in our recent study
including 56 patients with severe pulmonary embo-
lism, the lone patient who died had both pulmonary
embolism and stroke (Case 2).
1
It should be noted that stroke has been reported
after air travel even in the absence of deep venous
thrombosis or pulmonary embolism.
9,10 However, the
relation between stroke without pulmonary embo-
lism and air travel has never been demonstrated,
allowing us to imagine that such an event during air
travel might occur by chance alone.
Depending on whether respiratory or neurologic
systems compose the predominant clinical presenta-
tion, one of the diagnoses, stroke or pulmonary em-
bolism, might, in theory, be missed. This is a critical
problem because the interactions between these two
pathologies are important. Treatment of the patient
with concomitant pulmonary embolism and stroke
poses special risks. Thrombolysis and anticoagulant
therapy may aggravate brain injuries. Thus, a brain

infarct, if undiagnosed in the setting of predominant
respiratory symptoms, may become a life-threatening
event because of an increased bleeding risk due to
thrombolysis. Conversely, when neurologic injury dom-
inates the clinical presentation, undiagnosed pulmo-
nary embolism may be responsible for additional
1984 NEUROLOGY 60 June (2 of 2) 2003

thromboembolic events and aggravation of cerebral
hypoxia. Physicians therefore must be aware of the
potential of this association. In cases of severe pul-
monary embolism after air travel, a meticulous neu-
rologic examination should be accomplished to
eliminate the concomitant diagnosis of stroke. More-
over, in the case of a patient with neurologic deficit
after prolonged air travel, the diagnosis of pulmo-
nary embolism should be systematically considered.

The effects of cerebellar stimulation on motor cortex excitabil-

suppression and tremor score was found.
Tremor reset analysis was performed with five ET patients in
whom EMG tremor bursts could be distinguished reliably. Motor
cortex stimulation (resetting index of 0.97 /H110060.65) but not cerebel-

reset in ET (figure 2).
Discussion. The normal excitability of the cerebel-
lothalamocortical pathway in ET suggests that the
nature of cerebellar involvement in ET is different
from that in patients with lesions or atrophy of cere-
bellum or patients with lesions in the cerebellar out-
flow pathways. The findings also suggest that
thalamotomy or VIM DBS does not work by blocking
an overactive cerebellothalamocortical pathway.
However, these findings are still consistent with an
abnormal pattern of neural activity being transmit-
ted through the cerebellothalamocortical pathway,
and modulation of this activity by thalamotomy or
VIM DBS would lead to improvement in ET. Our
findings are also consistent with an oscillating
source feeding into the cerebellum,
7 and the inferior
olive has been implicated in this role. 2
Cerebellar stimulation sufficient to inhibit the
contralateral motor cortex did not reset tremor. One
explanation may be that the inferior olivary input to
the deep cerebellar nuclei may be more important
than the connection to the cerebellar cortex in medi-
ating ET
2 and the effects of cerebellar cortical stimu-
lation may be too weak to modify this rhythmicity.
Alternatively, the thalamocortical loop may be the
oscillator for ET, and cerebellar stimulation may be
insufficient to alter thalamocortical oscillation.

Case report. After a 3-year history of progressive stiffness of
the axial and leg muscles and painful spasms, this 30-year-old
man was diagnosed with SPS in 1990. Antibodies against glu-
tamic acid decarboxylase (antiGAD-Ab) were present in serum
(167,000 RIA [U]) and CSF (2,459 RIA [U]). Oral clonazepam,
baclofen, tizanidine, and valproic acid were not helpful. Immuno-
modulation treatment with corticosteroids, plasmapheresis, and
IV immunoglobulins achieved only temporary improvement. As
the disease progressed, the patient’s overall mobility declined con-
tinuously, and at age 35 years, he was mostly confined to a wheel-
chair. In December 1996, a programmable pump device
(Synchromed, Model 8615, Medtronic Inc., Minneapolis, MN) for
continuous ITB infusion was implanted. ITB resulted in a long-
lasting improvement, and the patient was able to walk short dis-
tances without crutches. During the first 2 years, the daily dosage
had to be gradually increased from 220 /H9262gt o6 3 2/H9262g to suppress
the spasms sufficiently. A stable period with a maintenance dos-
age of 632 /H9262g/d for some years followed. In December 2000, the
pump had to be replaced because of battery depletion. His mobil-
ity had remained stable during the past 5 years, and no substan-
tial autonomic disturbance was reported.
One day before admission, the patient developed progressive
bilateral leg spasms with a jerky onset. Spasms were elicited by
various stimuli, spread gradually to the back, abdomen, neck, and
arms, and frequently occurred in series with short pauses. Spas-
modic attacks were accompanied and often preceded by profuse
diaphoresis, hyperthermia (41 °C), arterial hypertension (210/110
mm Hg), and tachycardia (160 beats/min). Initially such attacks
lasted for up to 5 minutes, but within hours turned into an almost
continuous spasmodic storm. Repeated IV boluses of 10 mg diaze-
pam did not interrupt the spasmodic storm or the autonomic dis-
turbance. Progressive involvement of the diaphragm led to
respiratory failure; thus, mechanical ventilation was inevitable.
Despite the immediate infusion of midazolam (45 mg/h) and the
muscle relaxant atracurium (60 mg/h), the jerky spasms could not
be adequately suppressed, resulting in rhabdomyolysis with an
increase in serum creatine kinase levels (29,482 U/L). Within 1

and sepsis were excluded by normal CSF analysis and repeated
blood cultures. Because continuous, severe spasms developed as
soon as the myorelaxant was reduced, failure of the ITB delivery
system was suspected.
The pump was checked to exclude an error in programming or
in the filling status of the pump or the concentration of the ba-
clofen solution (2,000 /H9262g/mL). CSF could be aspirated easily
through the side port. Biplanar radiographic films showed that
the pump and catheter were in place. Programming a bolus to
produce a rotor movement of 90° demonstrated regular rotor func-
tion, and after an injection of 5 mL radiopaque solution through
the access port, the contrast medium entered the subarachnoid
space at the tip of the catheter without any obvious leakage.
On the supposition that the pump system was working cor-
rectly, the daily ITB dosage was gradually increased from 632 /H9262g
to 1200 /H9262g; however, this did not produce any significant improve-
ment. With high doses of sedatives and myorelaxants and the full
use of intensive care treatment, including dialysis and hemofiltra-
tion (3 weeks), mechanical ventilation (5 weeks), high-dose cat-
echolamines, and substitution of various blood components, the
patient’s clinical status stabilized, and he slowly began to recover.
Continuous IV administration of midazolam was replaced by an
oral medication of 3 /H110032 mg clonazepam, but the general muscle
stiffness could not be suppressed adequately, and the attacks of
myoclonic jerks and painful spasms required repeated IV boluses
of 0.5 mg clonazepam. Thus, surgical exploration of the pump
system was planned as soon as the patient’s condition had stabi-
lized sufficiently.
Open surgery revealed a small fissure in the catheter immedi-
ately beside the connector to the pump. Leakage of the drug oc-
curred only at a definite bending of the catheter (figure).

The patient’s catheter was 5-years-old,
and barium-impregnated catheters may become brittle
after 5 to 10 years. Thus, surgeons should consider
replacing them at the time of pump replacement.
Malfunction of the catheter system may occur in
up to 40% of patients receiving ITB.

kinks, and fibrosis of the catheter can often only be
detected by surgery. In 20% of instances, however,
even surgery fails to identify the cause of system
malfunction, but replacing the catheter still restores
the clinical response to ITB.
